parsed_output.analysis: The specification describes a top level human driving mode which is a simple state, an autonomous mode which is a composite/sub-machine, a Power On start into HumanDrivingMode, a guarded move HumanDrivingMode -> AutonomousMode on front_distance > 10, a return to HumanDrivingMode on human steering cmd, on brake pressed and on reaching the autonomous final substate, and a power-off termination to the system final state. The PlantUML model implements a Power On start, a simple HumanDrivingMode, a composite AutonomousMode with three unnamed substates and an explicit internal flow, a guarded HumanDrivingMode -> AutonomousMode transition, two Power Off transitions to [*], and a single composite-level transition AutonomousMode -> HumanDrivingMode guarded by “human steering cmd or brake pressed or in (auto final)”. The return-to-human-driving and the autonomous final substate handling, and the power-off termination are therefore not modelled as specified.

issues.issue: Return to HumanDrivingMode on reaching the autonomous final substate is not modelled as a transition from the final substate
issues.reason: The specification requires a transit to HumanDrivingMode when the autonomous sub-machine is in its auto final condition. The model instead terminates the sub-machine with SubState3 --> [*] inside AutonomousMode and provides a composite-level transition AutonomousMode --> HumanDrivingMode guarded by “in (auto final)”. That does not represent a transition originating from the final substate SubState3 to HumanDrivingMode and leaves the sub-machine ending in its internal final [*] with no defined target at the top level.
issues.where: AutonomousMode composite and the transition AutonomousMode --> HumanDrivingMode : human steering cmd\nor brake pressed\nor in (auto final) and SubState3 --> [*]

issues.issue: The return to HumanDrivingMode is modelled as a single composite-level transition with an OR guard for human steering cmd, brake pressed and ‘in (auto final)’
issues.reason: The specification lists human steering cmd, brake pressed and in (auto final) as conditions for a transit to HumanDrivingMode. The model collapses them into one composite exit guarded by an OR of the three, which allows a return to HumanDrivingMode from any autonomous substate on human steering cmd or brake pressed, not only in the context of the auto final substate as implied by the specification. The semantics of “in (auto final)” as a guard on a composite exit is not a proper state-based transition from the final substate.
issues.where: Transition AutonomousMode --> HumanDrivingMode : human steering cmd\nor brake pressed\nor in (auto final)

issues.reason: The specification only requires that autonomous mode has sub-states and is a sub-machine. It does not specify an automatic entry SubState1, the sequential progression SubState1->SubState2->SubState3, nor an internal final [*] that terminates the sub-machine. These explicit flows are not described in the specification and the internal final [*] conflicts with the required transition to HumanDrivingMode on auto final.
issues.where: state AutonomousMode { [*] --> SubState1; SubState1 --> SubState2; SubState2 --> SubState3; SubState3 --> [*] }

issues.issue: Power Off termination is modelled as two separate top-level exits instead of a single system final termination
issues.reason: The specification states ‘when power off, it will transit to final state’. The model provides two distinct Power Off transitions, one from HumanDrivingMode and one from the composite AutonomousMode. While functionally similar, the specification implies a single final termination behavior from any active state; the model does not provide a global power-off transition and the AutonomousMode exit does not explicitly cover being inside SubState1/2/3, relying on composite exit semantics.
issues.where: HumanDrivingMode --> [*] : Power Off and AutonomousMode --> [*] : Power Off

system_prompt:
You are an experienced control-systems engineer reviewing a state machine model against the natural-language specification it was built from.

You are given two things, both complete and unmodified:
  1. The natural-language specification.
  2. A state machine model written in PlantUML.

Your task: identify the places where the model does not conform to the specification. Read the specification in full first, then read the model in full, then report what you find.

Report as many or as few issues as you actually find, and organize them however you judge best. For each issue, state what the non-conformance is, which part of the model it concerns, and why you consider it a non-conformance.

Write your findings in en-US. Return only the requested structured response.
